description: The quintessential cereal grass of tropical Asia, cultivated in flooded paddy terraces and alluvial plains to nourish more than half of the human global population.
identifying_features: Erect annual clumping grass with hollow, jointed round culms up to 1-1.8 m tall
Long, flat linear leaf blades with rough scaberulous margins and a prominent membranous ligule
Arching terminal panicles bearing flattened one-flowered spikelets that mature into golden husked grains
habitat: Flooded wetland paddies, irrigated river deltas, and terraced hillside water basins.
distribution: Native to the Yangtze and Ganges river basins; cultivated across all rice belts of India and Asia.
uses: Staple dietary carbohydrate grain eaten steamed, boiled into khichdi, or ground into idli and dosa batter
Sacred grain (Akshata) used in every Hindu ritual, wedding blessing, and puja offering
Rice straw used for cattle fodder, thatched roofs, mushroom cultivation, and biodegradable paper
care_tips: Requires flooded or saturated muddy soil during vegetative tillering and panicle development
Thrives in hot, humid tropical climates with intense uninterrupted sunlight
Drain water from paddy fields 10-14 days before grain harvesting
toxicity_note: Non-toxic; raw husks are indigestible and must be milled. Cooked rice is one of the gentlest hypoallergenic foods known.
fun_fact: India is the world's largest exporter of rice, cultivating thousands of fragrant heritage varieties including the legendary long-grain Basmati and aromatic Gobindobhog.

description: The world's foremost cool-season temperate cereal grass, bearing dense awned spikes of golden grains that provide the flour foundation for rotis, breads, and pastas.
identifying_features: Upright annual tufted grass with hollow ribbed stems reaching 0.6 to 1.2 m in height
Flat, narrow linear leaves with clasping claw-like auricles at the junction of sheath and blade
Dense, erect terminal compound spikes with zigzag rachis bearing spikelets with or without bristly awns ('beards')
Oval golden-brown caryopsis grain with a deep longitudinal groove along one side
habitat: Irrigated winter farmlands, alluvial river plains (Indo-Gangetic plain), and temperate prairies.
distribution: Originated in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East; premier Rabi winter crop of northern India (Punjab, Haryana, UP).
uses: Milled into whole-wheat atta for daily rotis, chapatis, parathas, and refined maida for breads and bakery goods
Wheat straw (bhusa) serves as the primary winter dry livestock fodder across rural north India
Tender green wheatgrass juiced as an antioxidant-rich wellness beverage
care_tips: Sown as a winter (Rabi) crop in northern India, requiring cool vegetative temperatures and warm ripening weather
Needs well-drained, fertile alluvial or clay loam soil; cannot tolerate prolonged waterlogging
Requires 4-6 timed crown root irrigations during crucial growth stages
toxicity_note: Non-toxic; contains gluten proteins which cause immune reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.
fun_fact: Common bread wheat is an allohexaploid plant, meaning its complex genome contains six sets of chromosomes derived from three distinct ancestral wild grass species.

description: A robust, tall annual giant cereal grass with stout prop roots, broad arching leaves, terminal male tassel flowers, and ears of tightly packed sweet or starchy kernels.
identifying_features: Tall, solid, bamboo-like unbranched erect stalk reaching 2-3 meters in height, supported by stout aerial prop roots at base
Broad, wavy-margined linear leaves clasping the stem on alternating sides
Separate male and female flowers on same plant: terminal branching tassel (male) and axillary ear with silky styles (female)
Cylindrical cobs tightly wrapped in leafy husks, packed with rows of yellow, white, or multicolor grains
habitat: Agricultural grain fields, river terraces, and warm temperate-to-tropical croplands.
distribution: Domesticated in southern Mexico over 9,000 years ago; now cultivated extensively across India and worldwide.
uses: Fresh ears roasted over charcoal on Indian street carts (bhutta) with lime and black salt
Ground into yellow makki ka atta for iconic winter Makki ki Roti paired with Sarson ka Saag
Major global industrial source of cornstarch, corn syrup, poultry feed, and biofuel ethanol
care_tips: Requires full direct sun and rich, nitrogen-heavy, well-aerated soil
Plant in blocks of several short rows rather than single long rows to facilitate wind pollination
Keep consistently watered, particularly when tassels and silk emerge
toxicity_note: Non-toxic; corn kernels and silks are completely safe and edible for humans and domestic animals.
fun_fact: Every single strand of silk on an ear of corn connects to a single egg inside, meaning every single kernel on a cob must be individually pollinated by a grain of airborne pollen.

description: A gigantic, thick-stemmed perennial clumping grass with stout, jointed, fibrous stalks brimming with sweet sucrose-rich juice, grown as the world's primary sugar source.
identifying_features: Massive clumping stalks (culms) 3 to 5 meters tall and 3 to 5 cm thick, ringed with noticeable nodes
Stalks colored green, yellow, purple, or deep burgundy with sweet, fibrous, juice-saturated inner pith
Long, narrow, sword-like linear leaves with sharp serrulate edges and a pale prominent central midrib
Large, feathery, plume-like silvery-white terminal panicle known as an 'arrow'
habitat: Tropical and subtropical alluvial plains with high water availability and intense warmth.
distribution: Native to New Guinea and Southeast Asia; historically refined in India where crystalline sugar was invented.
uses: Stalks freshly crushed on Indian street stalls for refreshing sugarcane juice (Ganne ka ras) flavored with ginger and mint
Boiled and concentrated into traditional unrefined jaggery (gur) and refined crystalline table sugar
Bagasse fiber burned for thermal co-generation energy and molasses fermented into industrial ethanol
care_tips: Requires 10-12 months of hot tropical weather, high humidity, and copious irrigation
Prefers deep, rich, fertile loam or heavy clay soils with good drainage
Propagated vegetatively via stem cuttings ('setts') bearing at least 2-3 healthy eye buds
toxicity_note: Completely non-toxic; cane juice and jaggery are safe foods; moldy red-rot sugarcane should be avoided.
fun_fact: India was the first country in the world to invent the process of crystallizing sugarcane juice into solid crystals (Sanskrit: 'Khanda', origin of the English word 'candy') over 2,500 years ago.

description: An evergreen glossy-leaved shrub pruned into flat-topped bushes across rolling misty hills, whose tender young bud flushes yield black, green, oolong, and white teas.
identifying_features: Pruned flat-topped evergreen bushes (plucking tables) with dense, woody branching
Alternate, elliptic-to-lanceolate leathery glossy leaves with serrated margins and silky hairs on young flushes
Small, nodding, fragrant creamy-white flowers with 7-8 petals and a prominent cluster of bright yellow stamens
Three-lobed woody green-to-brown capsules containing round brown oily seeds
habitat: Misty subtropical mountain slopes, cool elevated plateaus, and acidic highland hill stations.
distribution: Native to East Asia and the Assam Brahmaputra valley of Northeast India; grown across Darjeeling, Assam, and Nilgiris.
uses: Harvesting 'two leaves and a bud' processed into world-renowned Darjeeling, Assam, and Nilgiri teas
Brewed as daily Indian spiced milk tea (Masala Chai) boiled with cardamom, ginger, and cloves
Rich in polyphenol antioxidants (EGCG), theanine, and gentle caffeine for mental clarity
care_tips: Requires strongly acidic, well-draining soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) rich in organic humus
Thrives under high rainfall, cool temperatures, and frequent misty humidity with morning sun
Requires regular plucking and pruning to maintain a dense vegetative flushing canopy
toxicity_note: Completely safe as a standard beverage. Highly concentrated botanical dietary supplements containing isolated epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) can cause rare idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity; caffeine and theophylline content makes tea toxic to dogs and cats.
fun_fact: All true teas — black, green, white, oolong, and pu-erh — come from the very same botanical species, Camellia sinensis; the dramatic differences in flavor and color arise solely from how the leaves are oxidized and processed.

sources.name: ASPCA Animal Poison Control & EFSA Scientific Opinion on Green Tea Catechins

description: A branching subtropical shrub bearing cream-to-pink mallow flowers, lobed leaves, and leathery green bolls that burst open at maturity to reveal snowy clouds of soft cellulose lint.
identifying_features: Erect, branching herbaceous shrub reaching 1 to 1.5 m with reddish hairy stems
Broad, palmately 3-to-5 lobed cordate leaves with hairy undersides and dark gland dots
Large, cup-shaped creamy-white or pale yellow flowers that turn dull pinkish-purple on the second day
Ovoid pointed green bolls that split into 3-5 valves, revealing fluffy white fibrous lint enclosing dark seeds
habitat: Warm, sunny agricultural river plains, black cotton soil tracts (Regur soils), and semi-arid valleys.
distribution: Native to Central America; widely cultivated throughout western and central India (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana).
uses: World's most important natural textile fiber ('white gold') woven into breathable cotton garments, towels, and bedsheets
Cottonseed crushed to extract edible cottonseed oil and high-protein livestock meal cake (khal)
Absorbent medical cotton wool used universally in wound dressings and surgical care
care_tips: Requires deep, moisture-retentive black basaltic soils (Regur) or fertile alluvial loam
Needs hot weather, full sun, and at least 180 to 200 frost-free sunny days
Keep dry and warm during boll bursting and lint harvesting to preserve fiber quality
toxicity_note: Purified fiber and refined cottonseed oil are safe. Raw unrefined cottonseed and foliage contain the toxic polyphenolic pigment gossypol, which causes severe myocardial necrosis, pulmonary edema, and male sterility in monogastric animals and humans.
fun_fact: Cotton fibers are practically pure natural cellulose (over 90%), arranged in hollow microscopic spirals that make them exceptionally soft, absorbent, and breathable.

sources.name: NCBI PubMed (Toxicol Appl Pharmacol / Kenar et al.)

description: A cool-season annual agricultural herb that carpets winter fields in sea of radiant canary-yellow 4-petaled blossoms, yielding pungent leaves and fiery oil-rich seeds.
identifying_features: Erect, smooth glaucous branching green stem up to 1-1.5 meters tall
Lower leaves are large, lyrate-pinnatifid with scalloped margins; upper leaves are smaller, lanceolate and sub-entire
Abundant terminal racemes of bright golden-yellow cruciform (4-petaled cross-shaped) flowers
Slender, cylindrical ascending silique pods (beaked pods) containing rows of tiny spherical reddish-brown seeds
habitat: Winter agricultural fields, alluvial riverbanks, and fertile northern plains.
distribution: Native to Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent; iconic winter crop of Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana, and Bengal.
uses: Pungent brown seeds cold-pressed into Kacchi Ghani mustard oil, the signature cooking oil of North and Eastern India
Tender winter leaves boiled and slow-simmered into Sarson ka Saag served with Makki ki Roti
Seeds ground into zesty kasundi and fish-curry pastes (Shorshe Ilish) in Bengal
care_tips: Grown as a winter Rabi crop; thrives in cool weather and full direct sunlight
Prefers well-drained loamy soil; sensitive to water stagnation during early root development
Harvest seed pods when plants turn golden-brown before pods shatter open
toxicity_note: Non-toxic in normal culinary use; mustard oil contains erucic acid and allyl isothiocyanate which gives it a pungent sharp bite. Safe and widely consumed.
fun_fact: The characteristic pungent nasal heat of mustard is only released when seeds or leaves are crushed in water, which activates the myrosinase enzyme to produce allyl isothiocyanate.

description: A sprawling, gland-dotted annual herb with aromatic dissected leaves, yellow star-shaped blossoms, and juicy red berries that are a cornerstone of modern world gastronomy.
identifying_features: Sprawling, glandular-pubescent weak stems covered in sticky hairs that release a strong, pungent odor
Pinnately divided leaves with irregular ovate, serrated leaflets
Clusters of nodding, star-shaped yellow flowers with reflexed petals and a conical yellow anther cone
Fleshy, juicy globose-to-oblong berries ripening from firm green to brilliant scarlet-red with multiple seed locules
habitat: Kitchen gardens, commercial vegetable farm plots, polyhouses, and terrace containers.
distribution: Native to western South America (Andes); now grown universally across India and worldwide.
uses: Essential savory flavor base for Indian gravies, curries, rasams, and fresh kachumber salads
Richest dietary source of the potent antioxidant carotenoid lycopene, supporting cardiovascular health
Processed commercially into tomato puree, ketchups, and canned sauces
care_tips: Requires at least 6-8 hours of direct sunshine and support trellising or tomato cages
Water deeply and consistently at the soil level; irregular watering causes blossom end rot and fruit splitting
Pinch out side-suckers from leaf axils on indeterminate varieties to focus energy on fruit ripening
toxicity_note: RIPE FRUIT IS SAFE AND EDIBLE. FOLIAGE AND GREEN UNRIPE FRUITS ARE TOXIC: Leaves, stems, and unripened green tomatoes contain toxic glycoalkaloids (solanine and tomatine). Ingestion of green plant parts can cause abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea in humans and pets.
fun_fact: Botanically, the tomato is a true berry, but a famous 1893 US Supreme Court case (Nix v. Hedden) legally classified it as a vegetable for taxation purposes because it is eaten as part of the main meal.

description: A bushy herbaceous plant producing solitary white star flowers and glossy elongated pods containing spicy capsaicin that gives heat and fire to Indian cuisine.
identifying_features: Bushy, angular-stemmed compact plant reaching 0.5 to 1 meter in height
Alternate, smooth, ovate-to-lanceolate leaves with entire margins and pointed tips
Solitary, nodding white or greenish-white star-like flowers borne in leaf axils
Glossy, elongated pendant or erect berries ripening from green to fiery crimson-red, packed with heat on placental membranes
habitat: Agricultural vegetable farms, sunny home gardens, and raised garden containers.
distribution: Native to Mesoamerica; introduced to India by Portuguese traders in the 16th century, now an inseparable national staple.
uses: Indispensable spice added fresh (hari mirch) or sun-dried and powdered (lal mirch) to almost all savory Indian dishes

Standardized topical capsaicin formulations are medically approved for relieving neuropathic pain in post-herpetic neuralgia and osteoarthritis through the depletion of substance P in sensory nerve terminals.
Traditional Indian protective amulets (nimbu-mirchi) hung to ward off the evil eye (nazar)
care_tips: Thrives in hot, sunny conditions with rich, well-draining garden soil
Water moderately; slightly restricting water during fruiting actually increases capsaicin heat intensity
Apply high-potash fertilizer when flower buds initiate
toxicity_note: Fruit is culinary safe; capsaicin is an intense mucous membrane irritant. Wash hands thoroughly after chopping; avoid touching eyes. Excessive intake can cause gastric pain. Keep away from household pets.
fun_fact: The fiery heat in chillies is measured on the Scoville Heat Scale; capsaicin does not cause an actual physical burn, but tricks sensory nerve endings into signaling extreme heat to the brain.

sources.name: NCBI PubMed (Cochrane Database Syst Rev / Derry et al.)

description: A robust, bushy annual vegetable herb bearing starry violet flowers and large, glossy, deep-purple fleshy berries beloved across India for hearty, tender roasted and curried dishes.
identifying_features: Bushy, coarse erect stem up to 1-1.5 m, sometimes armed with sharp prickles on calyx and stem
Large, alternate, coarsely lobed dull grey-green leaves covered in soft downy star-shaped hairs
Star-shaped violet or purple flowers with yellow central stamens clustered in leaf axils
Large, glossy, pear-shaped or globular berries with a persistent spiny green calyx and tender spongy white seed-flecked flesh
habitat: Fertile alluvial plains, homestead vegetable plots, and sunny agricultural farmlands.
distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia; cultivated across India since pre-Vedic antiquity.
uses: Charred and mashed over open flame to create the iconic smoky Baingan Bharta
Deep-fried in spiced gram-flour batter for Bengali Beguni, or stuffed in Maharashtrian Bharli Vangi
Excellent source of dietary fiber, nasunin anthocyanins in purple skin, and copper
care_tips: Requires hot, sunny weather and deep, fertile, organically rich loam soil
Stake heavy fruiting branches to keep heavy eggplants off wet soil
Harvest fruits while skin remains glossy; dull skin indicates overripe bitter seeds
toxicity_note: Cooked fruit is safe and nutritious. RAW FOLIAGE AND STEMS ARE TOXIC: Leaves and raw unripened fruit contain the toxic glycoalkaloid solanine; do not consume raw green parts or allow pets to chew foliage.
fun_fact: Botanical and linguistic records confirm that brinjal was domesticated in India over 4,000 years ago, and Sanskrit literature documents over 30 distinct historical culinary varieties.

description: A tall, erect warm-season annual herb with hibiscus-like pale yellow flowers and elongated ridged green seed pods prized for their tender texture and natural mucilaginous thickening.
identifying_features: Stout, erect semi-woody hairy stem growing 1 to 2 meters tall
Broad, palmately 5-to-7 lobed leaves with coarse serrated edges on long petioles
Showy, creamy-yellow hibiscus-like flowers with a deep dark-maroon or purple throat center
Elongated, ridged, tapering green pyramidal capsules filled with round white seeds and rich mucilage
habitat: Summer agricultural vegetable beds, warm alluvial loam fields, and kitchen gardens.
distribution: Native to tropical Africa and South Asia; enthusiastically cultivated as a daily staple vegetable across India.
uses: Staple Indian vegetable dish: dry-spiced stir-fry Bhindi Masala, Kurkuri Bhindi, or Bengali Dherosh Chorchori
Natural mucilage used as a thickener in traditional southern gumbos and stews
High natural source of soluble dietary fiber, Vitamin K, and folate
care_tips: Thrives in hot summer sunshine; seeds fail to germinate in cold or waterlogged soil
Plant in rich, well-draining garden soil enriched with mature compost
Harvest pods every 2-3 days while they are tender and snap easily; old pods become tough and stringy
toxicity_note: Completely non-toxic; pods, leaves, and seeds are edible and safe for humans and animals.
fun_fact: India is the world's undisputed king of okra production, harvesting over 60% of the entire global commercial okra crop each year.

description: The world's premier tuber crop, a sprawling nightshade family herb bearing starchy underground stem tubers that form the backbone of Indian street food and global cooking.
identifying_features: Sprawling herbaceous green stems with pinnately compound leaves composed of ovate leaflets
Clusters of white, pink, or pale lavender star-shaped flowers with bright yellow protruding anthers
Small, green tomato-like seed balls (berries) borne above ground containing true botanical seeds
Starchy underground stem tubers with protective corky skins and spirally arranged buds ('eyes')
habitat: Cool-season agricultural plains (Indo-Gangetic plain), temperate mountain slopes, and sandy loam beds.
distribution: Native to the South American Andes; introduced to India in the 17th century, now grown everywhere from UP to Bengal.
uses: Heart of Indian comfort cuisine: Aloo Gobi, Aloo Paratha, Samosa stuffing, Dum Aloo, and street chaat
Rich source of digestible dietary carbohydrates, potassium, and Vitamin B6
Commercial production of potato starch, flour, and snack chips
care_tips: Grown as a cool winter crop in the plains, or summer crop in the Himalayan hills
Requires loose, deeply tilled sandy loam soil to allow unhindered tuber expansion
Hill soil up around growing stems regularly to protect swelling tubers from sunlight exposure
toxicity_note: TUBERS ARE SAFE WHEN SOUND. GREEN PARTS AND SPROUTS ARE TOXIC: Green sun-exposed potato peel, green tubers, sprouts, and all aboveground foliage contain poisonous solanine and chaconine glycoalkaloids. Ingestion causes nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and headaches. NEVER eat green potatoes.
fun_fact: Potatoes are underground modified stems (tubers), not roots; the 'eyes' of a potato are actually dormant axillary buds capable of sprouting into new clonal plants.

description: A biennial pungent bulb herb with hollow cylindrical leaves, globose spherical umbels of starry white flowers, and layered fleshy underground bulbs indispensable in world cooking.
identifying_features: Hollow, cylindrical, glaucous bluish-green leaves growing in a fan from the underground basal stem plate
Layered underground bulb composed of concentric fleshy modified leaf bases enclosed in dry, papery brown-to-purple tunics
Tall, hollow flowering scape topped by a dense spherical umbel of small white or pale greenish flowers
Strong, pungent lachrymatory aroma released when bulb cells are ruptured or sliced
habitat: Agricultural crop fields, market vegetable gardens, and alluvial vegetable terraces.
distribution: Native to Central/Southwestern Asia; grown in colossal quantities across Maharashtra (Nashik), Gujarat, and nationwide.
uses: Fundamental aromatic flavor foundation for Indian tadkas, gravies, biryanis, and salads
High natural source of quercetin, a powerful antioxidant flavonoid supporting cellular health

Folk remedy for hair thinning; a pilot clinical trial showed crude topical onion juice promoted hair regrowth in patchy alopecia areata due to high sulfur and flavonoid content, though further large-scale validation is needed.
care_tips: Needs full direct sun and fertile, loose, sandy loam soil free of rocks
Keep soil weed-free and uniformly moist during early bulb swelling; withhold water as tops flop over
Allow harvested bulbs to dry and cure in a well-ventilated shaded space for several weeks
toxicity_note: SAFE FOR HUMANS. TOXIC TO PETS: Contains organosulfoxides and N-propyl disulfide that are highly toxic to dogs, cats, and horses, destroying red blood cells and triggering life-threatening hemolytic anemia.
fun_fact: Onions make you cry because slicing cell walls mixes sulfenic acids with enzymes to create syn-propanethial-S-oxide gas, which reacts with tear-duct moisture to form mild sulfuric acid.

description: A feathery, aromatic annual herb whose refreshing citrus-herbal leaves (cilantro) and warm, spicy-citrus dried spherical seeds (coriander) are central to Indian cookery.
identifying_features: Slender, erect hollow branching stems up to 30-60 cm tall
Dimorphic foliage: broad, fan-lobed lower leaves and finely dissected feathery upper leaves
Compound umbels of tiny white to pale pinkish asymmetric flowers
Globose, ribbed, hollow dual-seeded schizocarps turning from green to fragrant straw-brown
habitat: Sunny vegetable beds, alluvial winter croplands, and kitchen herb pots.
distribution: Native to the Mediterranean and southwestern Asia; widely cultivated in Rajasthan, Gujarat, and across India.
uses: Fresh chopped leaves (cilantro / green dhaniya) used as the universal finishing garnish on all Indian curries and dals
Dry roasted seeds ground into dhaniya powder, a foundational warm spice in garam masala and curry powders

Classical Ayurvedic cold infusion of crushed seeds (Dhaniya hima) is recognized by the European Medicines Agency as a traditional herbal medicine for symptomatic relief of mild spasmodic gastrointestinal complaints.
care_tips: Thrives in cool weather and morning sun; rapidly bolts to flower in hot, dry conditions
Keep soil evenly moist using well-aerated, fertile potting loam
Sow successive seeds every 3 weeks for an uninterrupted supply of fresh tender leaves
toxicity_note: Non-toxic and edible; a harmless genetic variation in OR6A2 olfactory receptor genes causes cilantro to taste intensely like soap to about 10-15% of people.
fun_fact: Every part of the coriander plant is edible — the tender leafy greens (cilantro), the flowers, the dried seeds (coriander), and even the pungent roots which form the base of Thai curry pastes.

description: A cool-season leafy annual vegetable forming basal rosettes of succulent, deep-green tender leaves celebrated worldwide for their rich iron, folate, and vitamin content.
identifying_features: Basal rosette of succulent, deep-green, ovate to triangular-hastate leaves with prominent veins
Leaves can be smooth-flat or deeply crinkled (savoy)
Dioecious flowering (male and female flowers on separate plants) producing tiny greenish apetalous clusters on upright spikes
Compact cluster of small hard, spiny or smooth fruits enclosing seeds
habitat: Cool-season vegetable plots, raised kitchen garden beds, and fertile agricultural loams.
distribution: Native to ancient Persia (central and western Asia); universally cultivated across India as a premier winter leafy green.
uses: Blanched and pureed with paneer into the beloved restaurant classic Palak Paneer
Stir-fried with potatoes in Aloo Palak or simmered into comforting Bengali Palang Shaker Ghonto
Rich in lutein, zeaxanthin, iron, folate, and Vitamins A, C, and K
care_tips: Requires cool temperatures (10-22°C); hot weather immediately triggers bitter flowering stalks (bolting)
Provide full winter sun and nitrogen-rich, moisture-retentive, well-draining garden soil
Harvest outer leaves continuously (cut-and-come-again) to prolong the vegetative harvest window
toxicity_note: Wholesome and nutrient-dense in dietary amounts. High concentrations of soluble oxalic acid can bind dietary minerals and dramatically increase urinary oxalate excretion, posing a significant risk of calcium oxalate urolithiasis in susceptible individuals.
fun_fact: The famous myth that spinach contains astronomical amounts of iron originated from a 19th-century German chemist who misplaced a decimal point, attributing tenfold the actual iron content to the leaf.

sources.name: NCBI PubMed (Am J Clin Nutr / Chai & Liebman) & Harvard Health
